title: The priest and the hunter
hook: the temple priest, and the hunter whose love Shiva saw
carry: the priest offers the form; you bring the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina, walking around the holy. Your line was keep the holy at the center.
screen: `PRADAKSHINA — KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: In the hills of Kalahasti, in South India, the story goes, a temple priest came each morning to a lonely shrine of Shiva. He bathed the lingam, decorated it, chanted every verse exactly. And each morning he found a mess: his flowers pushed aside, meat left on the stone, the lingam wet with water someone had carried in their mouth. The someone was a young hunter named Thinnan. He knew no Sanskrit and no rules. He simply loved Shiva at first sight, and brought him what he had: water in his mouth, flowers from his own hair, the best meat from the hunt, tasted first. Today: the priest, and the hunter.
screen: `A PRIEST, A PERFECT RITE.` → `A HUNTER WITH NO RULES.` → `HE BRINGS WHAT HE HAS.`

segments.voice: Shiva told the heartbroken priest in a dream: hide, and watch. The next day the hunter came, and the priest saw blood running from one eye of the lingam. He cut out his own eye with an arrow and pressed it onto the bleeding one, and the bleeding stopped. Then the other eye began to bleed. He set his foot on the spot so he wouldn't lose it, and raised the arrow to his second eye. And Shiva's voice stopped him: stop, Kannappa. He's been Kannappa ever since, one of the sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva in the Periya Puranam. The story doesn't throw out the priest: Shiva showed him the hunter's love. The priest's word is pujari, the one who does the puja. In many temples only priests enter the inner shrine, and they care for the murti every day: bathing it, dressing it, feeding it, arti, by rules handed down for generations. And when you bring an offering, he makes it for you. He asks your name, often your family line, and sets them into the Sanskrit: who is offering, when, and why. That's the sankalpa. Then he recites the deity's names, often a hundred and eight, a flower with each: archana. The priest keeps the form exact, and the offering is still yours. You don't have to know every word. Kannappa didn't know one, and Shiva received what he brought. That love has a name: bhakti.
screen: `KANNAPPA GIVES HIS EYE.` · `STOP, KANNAPPA.` · `PUJARI — THE ONE WHO DOES THE PUJA.` · `SANKALPA, ARCHANA, AND YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Take one small thing within reach: a flower, a glass of water, a sweet, even a leaf. Hold it before your shrine, or just in front of you. Make your own sankalpa, in your own words: your name, today's date, and what you're offering it for. Then offer it, the way Kannappa did, with whatever you have. If you don't pray, say your name and one thing you'll give your whole heart to today, and set the thing down gently.
Pujari. The temple priest: he keeps the rites exact, and offers on your behalf, with your name inside. Today's word.
Your line: the priest offers the form; you bring the heart. Kannappa had only his heart. See you tomorrow.

screen: `THE PRIEST OFFERS THE FORM; YOU BRING THE HEART.` → `DAY 135 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TUKARAM AND THE BHAJAN.`

howItsDone: In Hindu temples, the pujari performs the daily rites for the deity (bathing, dressing, food offerings and arti), and on request performs archana on a devotee's behalf, opening with a sankalpa that names the worshipper; the Tamil saint Kannappa, the hunter who offered his own eye, is honored at the Kalahasti temple.

pujari.meaning: the temple priest, the one who does the puja

Kannappa.meaning: a hunter-saint of Shiva who offered his own eye; the name comes from the Tamil for eye

sankalpa.meaning: stating who is offering, when, and why, at the start of a rite

archana.meaning: offering a flower with each of the deity's names

murti.meaning: the sacred image, cared for like someone living in the house

notes: The hook describes a common South Indian temple scene (white cloth, sacred thread); dress varies by region.

The script says most temple priests have traditionally come from Brahmin families and that some temples and groups now train priests from other backgrounds, including women (e.g., Kerala's Travancore Devaswom Board appointments, 2017; training programs in Maharashtra).
